summary:
Compute economics and ops lens. Rented GPUs are now cheap: an RTX 4090 costs about $0.33-0.60/h on demand and a 5090 about $0.35-0.99/h. An A100-80GB on vast.ai is about $0.40-1.40/h, and an H100 about $1.30-3.50/h. Colab Pro buys roughly 18 A100-40GB hours for $10, or about 84 T4 hours. So compute stops being a constraint for Enveda-scale models: fingerprint heads and DreaMS/MIST-size transformers of about 100M parameters, trained on about 2.5M spectra.

The best value is a single 24-32 GB consumer card (4090/5090) on vast.ai or RunPod Community Cloud. Such a card is about 4-6x a Kaggle T4 per hour (estimate), so one T4-equivalent hour costs about $0.08-0.15.

Recommended budget: about $50 by default, raised to about $150 only if a GPU-trained feature beats our honest CV on masks B and C. Spending $400 buys capacity we cannot use, because attention (people-hours and a clean CV) stays the binding constraint, exactly as in Biohub. There, quota never ran out: 26.7 h were free on 23 Sep.

Effect on odds (estimate): extra compute moves Enveda from bronze ~30-40% / silver ~10% to roughly bronze ~35-45% / silver ~12-15%. The gain comes from faster iteration (overnight 4090 runs instead of 12 h T4 sessions), seed ensembles and a full DreaMS fine-tune, not from any single big model. Gold stays unrealistic. Rentals do not rescue RSNA Knee (570 GB of data, entry by 15 Oct, saturated top) or ARC.

Rentals make a Gemma-4 31B QLoRA run technically possible, at about $20-60 per run on one 80 GB card (estimate). The Gemma odds are still capped by scoring noise and the unverified claim that the scorer drops adapters, so it stays on watch.

The friend's 5070 Ti (16 GB) is a good free overnight box for every Enveda model we plan, at about 0.6-0.7x a 4090 (estimate). It must stay off the critical path, and it needs PyTorch cu128+ wheels (Blackwell sm_120).

Ops recipe: one pinned CUDA 12.8+ image, SSH from Windows, data sent from the laptop by scp or kept on a network volume, checkpoints synced off the box every 20-30 min, and a self-stop at the end of each script. Prepaid credits are the only way to pay; stop the instance, then destroy it and its volume. No Kaggle token on community hosts. Weights go into Kaggle as a private dataset or model that the user uploads from his laptop. Train in bf16 and run inference in fp16/fp32 on a Kaggle T4.

findings.claim: RunPod list prices (30 Sep 2026), Community vs Secure Cloud per GPU-hour: RTX 3090 $0.22/$0.50; RTX 4090 $0.34/$0.74; RTX 5090 $0.69/$0.99; L4 $0.44/$0.49; RTX A6000 $0.33/$0.53; L40S $0.79/$1.09; A100 PCIe $1.19/$1.59; A100 SXM $1.39/$1.59; H100 PCIe $1.99/$2.89; H100 SXM $2.69/$3.49. Storage: container disk $0.10/GB-mo, volume $0.10/GB-mo while running and $0.20 while idle, network volume $0.07/GB-mo. The pricing page lists no spot tier.

findings.claim: vast.ai is a marketplace with variable prices, and it is the cheapest option overall. Tracker snapshots from 30 Sep 2026: RTX 4090 about $0.33/h on demand and from $0.11/h spot (another tracker gives $0.31 spot, $0.56 on demand); RTX 5090 spot from $0.20/h; A100 PCIe 40GB about $0.60/h; A100 SXM 80GB about $0.67/h (cheapest on-demand A100 $0.40, spot $0.29); H100 SXM from $1.47/h on demand and from $0.36/h spot; L40S from $0.80/h. Treat all of these as estimates: offers change hourly and host reliability varies.

findings.claim: Colab: Free gives a T4 with no guarantee, sessions of about 12 h at most and a disconnect after about 90 min idle. Pro costs $9.99/month for 100 compute units (CU). Pro+ costs $49.99/month for 500 CU (one source says 600, so verify on colab.research.google.com/signup) and adds background execution. Extra units cost $9.99 per 100 CU. Measured burn: T4 ~1.19 CU/h (~84 h per 100 CU, ~$0.12/h), L4 ~1.71 (~58 h, ~$0.17/h), A100-40GB ~5.4 (~18 h, ~$0.54/h), A100-80GB ~7.5 (~13 h, ~$0.75/h). Units are a budget, not a reservation: premium GPUs may be unavailable, and sessions can be cut.
findings.evidence: https://www.thundercompute.com/blog/colab-alternatives-for-cheap-deep-learning-in-2025 (Sep 2025, CU rates measured Mar 2026 per search snippet) ; https://aicoolies.com/pricing/google-colab

findings.claim: Kaggle gives about 30 GPU-h per account per week (P100 or 2xT4), which is about 320 h over 10.7 weeks. Each session lasts at most 12 h, so long training needs checkpoint and resume. On the ARC competitions, L4x4 machines count double against the quota; that is stated on the ARC overview pages and does not affect Enveda. In Biohub the quota never ran out (26.7 h free on 23 Sep, about 55-60 GPU-h used in total). The teammates' quotas, about 30 h/week each, went mostly unused.
findings.evidence: https://www.kaggle.com/docs/efficient-gpu-usage ; research/next_competition/raw.json (ARC L4x4 note from /overview) ; research/postmortem/why_no_trained_models_ru.md §2.6, §2.4

findings.claim: Enveda-scale workloads are small by rental standards (estimates). DreaMS embeddings of 1M spectra take about 1 h on an A100 (published), so all ~2.5M training spectra take about 2.5 A100-h, about 3-4 h on a 4090 (under $2) or about 10-15 T4-h. A head on frozen embeddings is minutes to an hour. A full DreaMS or MIST-style fingerprint fine-tune is about 10-20 A100/4090-h per run (earlier estimate: 20-60 T4-class h). DiffMS (the class-C de novo model) fine-tunes at 46 min/epoch on a 2080Ti on MassSpecGym, 15 epochs, so about 11.5 h. At our data scale that is about 30-40 4090-h per run, for 2.3% top-1 on MassSpecGym: low priority.
findings.evidence: DreaMS throughput: Nature Biotech 2025 https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-025-02663-3 (via search snippet); DiffMS compute and accuracy: https://arxiv.org/html/2502.09571v2 ; DreaMS weights MIT on Zenodo/HF https://github.com/pluskal-lab/DreaMS ; MIST MIT with checkpoints https://github.com/samgoldman97/mist

findings.claim: Relative speed for bf16/fp16 training of about 100M-parameter models, rough and data-loader-bound (estimate): T4 or P100 = 1x, L4 ~1.5-2x, 5070 Ti ~2.5-3.5x, 4090 ~4-6x, 5090 ~5-8x, A100 ~5-8x, H100 ~10-15x. By cost per T4-equivalent hour, 4090 and 5090 on vast or RunPod Community (~$0.07-0.15) and Colab Pro A100 (~$0.08) are best. H100s only pay off for models over 24-32 GB (Gemma 31B), not for Enveda.
findings.evidence: Derived from dense tensor TFLOPS (T4 65, L4 121, 4090 ~165, A100 312, H100 SXM ~989 fp16/bf16) and the prices above; an estimate, not a benchmark

findings.claim: Hidden costs: storage keeps billing while an instance is stopped (RunPod idle volume $0.20/GB-mo; vast charges disk on stopped instances). vast hosts may charge per-TB bandwidth. Each new box costs about 30-60 min of setup. An interruptible instance can be paused by a higher bid and lose any work since the last checkpoint. Budget a 20-30% overhead on paper GPU-hour estimates (estimate). The biggest real risk is a forgotten running box: a 4090 left on for a week costs about $55-80.
findings.evidence: https://www.runpod.io/pricing ; https://docs.vast.ai/documentation/reference/faq/instances

findings.claim: Auto-shutdown is available on both platforms. vast injects CONTAINER_ID and a per-instance CONTAINER_API_KEY, so a script can end with `vastai stop instance $CONTAINER_ID` (or `destroy`). RunPod injects RUNPOD_POD_ID and a scoped key, so `runpodctl stop pod $RUNPOD_POD_ID` works, and `sleep 10h; runpodctl stop pod $RUNPOD_POD_ID &` makes a dead-man timer. Neither needs the user's account key on the box.
findings.evidence: https://docs.vast.ai/cli/reference/stop-instance ; https://docs.vast.ai/documentation/reference/faq/instances ; https://docs.runpod.io/pods/manage-pods ; https://github.com/runpod/runpodctl/blob/main/docs/runpodctl_stop_pod.md

findings.claim: The friend's RTX 5070 Ti (16 GB, Blackwell sm_120) needs CUDA 12.8+ and cu128 PyTorch wheels (`pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128`); older cu12.4 builds fail with 'no kernel image'. 16 GB fits every Enveda model we plan: DreaMS or MIST fine-tunes and heads in bf16 at batch 64-256, and DiffMS fine-tunes (the paper ran them on 12 GB 2080Tis) (estimate). It does not fit Gemma 31B QLoRA. The same CUDA 12.8 image should be used everywhere so code moves between the 5070 Ti, rentals and Colab. In Biohub the friends' cards were unavailable mid-competition, so this box goes only to seeds and sweeps, never to the critical path.
findings.evidence: https://discuss.pytorch.org/t/nvidia-geforce-rtx-5070-ti-with-cuda-capability-sm-120/221509 ; https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/164342 ; DiffMS paper (2080Ti 12 GB) ; why_no_trained_models_ru.md §2.4

findings.claim: Moving weights into a code competition: the user uploads them from his laptop as a private Kaggle Dataset or Kaggle Model and attaches it to the offline submission notebook. The standard rule, not verified for Enveda (the rules page did not render without login, so the user should read it), allows own weights as the team's work product, while external data and pretrained models must be public and free to all. DreaMS and MIST (MIT, on Zenodo/HF) qualify. Whether the derived PubChem candidate pool must be a public dataset or may stay private is a rules question to settle before building it. Publishing needs the user's yes either way.
findings.evidence: Kaggle standard competition rules (External Data / Winner License sections, general knowledge); fetch of https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/enveda-CASMI26-molecule-id-mass-spectra/rules returned only the title

findings.claim: Inference pitfalls on Kaggle: the T4 has no native bf16, so a model trained in bf16 on a 4090 or 5070 Ti should be exported and run in fp16 or fp32 on the T4, or on CPU. Recent cu128+ PyTorch builds may lack Pascal (P100, sm_60) kernels (to be checked), so the T4 is the target. The test is only about 1,500 spectra, so model inference is minutes. The 9 h limit is driven by candidate retrieval and scoring, not by the network.
findings.evidence: NVIDIA T4 (sm_75) lacks bf16 tensor cores; PyTorch release notes on dropping older archs in CUDA 12.8 builds (to verify); test size from raw.json /data summary

findings.claim: Security for a Windows user: create an ed25519 SSH key with Windows OpenSSH and paste only the public key into the provider console (the user does this). Work in tmux over SSH or VS Code Remote-SSH. Never put the Kaggle token on community-cloud hosts, which are third-party machines. Move weights box -> laptop (scp or a private HF repo with a fine-grained token scoped to one repo) -> Kaggle, with the user uploading. Keep .env, kaggle.json and *.token in .gitignore and put secrets in the provider's secret store or the shell only. Pay only with prepaid credit (vast is prepaid; RunPod uses a balance), topped up $25 at a time. Destroy instances and volumes after copying out, and rotate any token that touched a box when the competition ends. Competition data goes only to private storage or scp, never to a public bucket; the rules forbid redistribution.
findings.evidence: Standard practice; Kaggle rules on data redistribution (general); user policy that the assistant never enters credentials (task RULES)

numbers:
All figures are estimates unless marked as a list price.

Prices per GPU-hour (list or tracker, 30 Sep 2026):
- RTX 4090: vast $0.11 spot, $0.31-0.56 on demand; RunPod Community $0.34, Secure $0.74.
- RTX 5090: vast from $0.20 spot; RunPod $0.69 / $0.99; median $0.64.
- A100-80GB: vast ~$0.40-0.67; RunPod $1.19-1.59; Lambda A100-40GB $1.99.
- H100: vast $0.36 spot, ~$1.47 on demand; RunPod $1.99-3.49; Lambda $3.29-4.29; median $3.39.
- L40S: $0.79-1.09.
- Colab: Pro $9.99 for 100 CU; Pro+ $49.99 for 500 CU (600 per one source); T4 ~$0.12/h, L4 ~$0.17/h, A100-40GB ~$0.54/h, A100-80GB ~$0.75/h.
- Kaggle: free, about 30 h/week, about 320 h over 10.7 weeks per account.

Throughput in T4-equivalents (estimate): 5070 Ti ~3x, 4090 ~5x, A100 ~6x, H100 ~12x.

Budget scenarios over ~10 weeks (T4-eq = T4-equivalent hours; estimate):
- $0: Kaggle ~320 T4-h, plus free Colab T4 opportunistically, plus the 5070 Ti overnight (~3x T4) when available. Total about 400-600 T4-eq h. Enough for DreaMS embeddings (~10-15 T4-h) plus a head, 1-2 full fingerprint fine-tunes on 12 h checkpointed sessions, and a small sweep. The price is slow iteration: 1-2 runs per week.
- ~$50: about 100-150 h of 4090 (500-700 T4-eq), or Colab Pro for 1 month plus ~$40 on vast. Enough for 3-5 full fingerprint fine-tunes (DreaMS FT or MIST), 3-seed ensembles, and a 10-20 config head sweep. Overnight turnaround. Recommended default.
- ~$150: about 300-400 h of 4090/5090, or ~150-200 h of A100-80GB. Adds a contrastive spectrum-molecule retrieval model, 5+ model ensembles, and 1-2 DiffMS fine-tunes for class C (~30-40 4090-h each) as an experiment. Only after a CV gate.
- ~$400: about 150-250 H100-h or ~800-1,000 4090-h. Continued self-supervised pretraining of DreaMS on timsTOF (enveda-180, 1.15M spectra), large ensembles, de novo generation. Likely diminishing returns for us.
- Gemma 31B QLoRA, if ever: one 80 GB card, ~10-20 h per run, ~$20-60 per run.

Odds (estimate): Enveda bronze 30-40% becomes ~35-45%; silver 10% becomes ~12-15%; gold <3%. Gemma bronze stays ~10-20% (noise-limited). RSNA and ARC stay skipped.
plan:
Plan from the compute and ops lens. Money follows the CV; the GPU never leads.

Week 1-2 (to ~14 Oct): $0.
- All CPU work on the laptop: metric, three-mask CV on np-examples, public-notebook baseline, candidate pool, LightGBM LambdaRank.
- In parallel, build one reproducible training kit: a pinned CUDA 12.8+ PyTorch image or environment file, `train.py` with checkpoint and resume (model, optimizer, scheduler, RNG, step) every 20-30 min, a metadata JSON per checkpoint (git hash, config, seed, data hash, pip freeze), and a self-stop line at the end.
- Smoke-test it for 30 min each on Kaggle, free Colab and, if available, the 5070 Ti.
- The user opens accounts on vast.ai and/or RunPod, adds an SSH public key and puts in $25 of prepaid credit. The assistant never touches credentials.

Week 2-3: <$5.
- Compute DreaMS embeddings for all train spectra on Kaggle (~10-15 h) or on one 4090 hour-block (~$2). Train a fingerprint or retrieval head on them.
- Gate 1: does the head feature raise MRR on masks B and C beyond noise across the three masks? If not, stop GPU spending and invest in retrieval and features instead.

Week 3-6: up to ~$50.
- If Gate 1 passes, run full DreaMS or MIST fine-tunes on a rented 4090/5090 overnight (interruptible where checkpointing is solid, ~$3-8 per run). Seeds and sweeps go to the 5070 Ti and Kaggle quota.
- One approved LB probe per major CV jump to calibrate CV against LB.

Week 6-8: up to ~$150, only if Gate 2 passes.
- Gate 2: the ensemble or second model adds on CV.
- Then: an ensemble of 3-5 models, optionally a contrastive retrieval model, and at most one DiffMS class-C experiment.
- Also check Gemma go/no-go on 20 Oct: a rented 80 GB card makes one QLoRA run affordable (~$20-60), but enter only if the other conditions in judge.md hold.

Week 9-10: freeze.
- A final reproducible training run from a clean image.
- The user uploads the weights as a private Kaggle Dataset or Model from the laptop (a publication only if the rules force it, and only with his yes).
- Dry-run the offline inference notebook on a T4 in fp16/fp32 under 9 h.
- Destroy all instances and volumes and rotate tokens.

Standing rules:
- Prepaid only, with a spend log in CONTEXT.md (date, box, hours, $, run id).
- A dead-man stop timer on every box.
- No Kaggle token on third-party hosts.
- Minimal Kaggle API use: send data to boxes by scp from the laptop, not with `kaggle download` on each box.
- One person owns the model line with continuous time, the main Biohub lesson.

summary:
Short answer: with extra compute, only Gemma 4 Developer Agent really gets better. The main reason is not training. We can rent one 80 GB GPU and serve the exact scored checkpoint (google/gemma-4-31B-it-qat-w4a16-ct) in vLLM, which cuts one honest CV pass from 8-12 Kaggle GPU-h to about $3-8 and 1.5-3 h (estimate). That removes the "measurement is too expensive" dealbreaker. Gemma rises from fit 4.5 to about 6/10 and becomes the only credible SECOND competition next to Enveda, still gated around 14-20 Oct. The private set of about 60 tasks is still a lottery, and whether LoRA works at all is doubtful: vLLM issue #41754 (Unsloth Gemma 4 adapters ignored, still open) and an unverified claim that the scorer wipes adapters.

RSNA Knee: rented GPUs remove the GPU wall (about 100-150 GPU-h for roughly $100-400, estimate). They do not remove the real blockers: 22 days, entry by 15 Oct, only 58 gold-labelled studies (so honest CV is too noisy), and a top 50 already saturated at 0.953-0.961. It would also take all our attention during Enveda's critical first three weeks. Fit rises only to about 3.5, and the verdict stays SKIP.

ARC-AGI-2/3: scoring runs on Kaggle anyway. Rented 4×L4 or H100 time makes dev and CV runs cheap (ARC-2 about $13-21 per 12 h run; ARC-3 about $3-15 per 25-game pass, estimates). But neither has an honest CV: ARC-3's 25 public games do not predict the 55 private ones. For ARC-2, an own model at NVARC scale (reportedly about 864 H100-h for fine-tuning alone) does not fit in 33 days. Both stay "no as a second competition". The only exception is an ARC-2 fork ticket submitted early by a teammate, and only with the user's yes. Compute is worth much more inside Enveda (training our own spectrum-to-fingerprint model) than in any of these three.

findings.claim: Prices for rented GPUs, which drive all the cost estimates below: H100 80GB about $1.5-2.7/h, A100 80GB about $0.7-1.4/h, L4 about $0.27-0.44/h. Colab A100 is about $0.5-1.1/h.
findings.evidence: Vast.ai: H100 on-demand about $1.76/h; verified hosts $1.49-2.27/h; A100 80GB average about $0.72/h (https://www.spheron.network/blog/vastai-pricing-2026/, https://intuitionlabs.ai/articles/h100-rental-prices-cloud-comparison, https://medium.com/@velinxs/cheap-a100-rentals-find-the-best-deals-in-2026-ddeae320a324). RunPod Community: H100 PCIe $1.99/h, SXM $2.69/h, A100 $1.19-1.39/h; no data-transfer fees; storage $0.05-0.20/GB-month (https://www.runpod.io/pricing, https://northflank.com/blog/runpod-gpu-pricing). Lambda: H100 $3.29/h, A100 80GB $2.79/h (https://lambda.ai/pricing). L4: vast.ai from $0.27/h, RunPod $0.44/h (https://vast.ai/pricing/gpu/L4, https://getdeploying.com/gpus/nvidia-l4). Colab: $9.99 per 100 CU; A100 burns about 5-11 CU/h (https://mccormickml.com/2024/04/23/colab-gpus-features-and-pricing/, https://varlog.info/colab-credit-consumption-comparison-2024/). Marketplace prices move daily; treat all of these as snapshots.

findings.claim: Gemma: the biggest change is cheap, faithful CV, not LoRA. On a rented 80 GB GPU we can serve the exact scored checkpoint in vLLM, so one pass over the 129 train tasks costs about $3-8 instead of 8-12 Kaggle GPU-h (estimate).
findings.evidence: The checkpoint is public on Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/google/gemma-4-31B-it-qat-w4a16-ct. A third-party repo (unverified) says the scorer serves it with vLLM at 32k context on 4× L4, with about 12 h for about 120 tasks (https://github.com/Gosling-dude/gemma4-developer-agent). Another repo quotes a per-task budget of 60 min and 100 tool calls (https://github.com/emiliodavola/kaggle-gemma-agent). My estimate: 8-16 tasks run concurrently with vLLM prefix caching on 1× H100, so a pass takes about 1.5-3 h, which at $1.5-2.7/h is about $3-8. A timing check on a rented 4× L4 copy of the scorer costs about 12 h × $1.1-1.8/h = $13-21. Thirty passes cost about $100-250. That makes 2-3 repeats per config affordable, which the run-to-run noise requires.

findings.claim: Gemma: the 5070 Ti and Colab do not help much. 16 GB cannot serve the 31B w4a16 model, and Colab cannot run the Docker sandboxes the harness needs. Use a vast.ai VM instance or a Lambda VM, or keep the harness on the laptop (WSL2) and connect it to a rented vLLM server.
findings.evidence: My estimate: about 15.5 GB of 4-bit weights plus about 2-3 GB of bf16 embeddings (262k vocabulary) plus KV cache is more than 16 GB. RunPod pods do not support Docker-in-Docker; vast.ai VM instances do (https://docs.vast.ai/linux-virtual-machines, https://www.runpod.io/blog/enhanced-cpu-pods-docker-network, https://github.com/skypilot-org/skypilot/issues/3096). The user sets up any server tokens himself.

findings.claim: Gemma LoRA is now affordable, about $15-100 of rented GPU (estimate). Whether the scorer actually applies adapters is doubtful, so it must be tested with one approved submission before we invest.
findings.evidence: Unsloth says QLoRA of Gemma 4 31B needs about 22 GB of VRAM. That rules out the 5070 Ti but works on 1× A100/H100 (https://unsloth.ai/docs/models/gemma-4/train). Adapters must be .safetensors and under 3 GiB in total (emiliodavola repo). vLLM issue #41754, opened 5 May 2026 and still open: Unsloth LoRA adapters for Gemma 4 load but have no effect on the output (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/41754). The Gosling-dude repo claims 'adapters are wiped by the scorer's patched vLLM' (unverified). There is also a mismatch: the adapter would be trained on a bf16 or QAT base and scored on the w4a16 checkpoint. The test: one submission, with the user's yes, using a deliberately behaviour-changing adapter.

findings.claim: Gemma: the lottery does not go away. Cheap CV reduces our own selection error, but private rank over about 60 tasks is still noisy. New fit about 6/10 (was 4.5). Bronze about 20-30% (was 10-20%), silver about 6-10%, gold under 2% (estimates). Silver about 10-15% only if the LoRA test is positive.
findings.evidence: At p=0.15 and n=60, the standard error is about 2.8 tasks, about 4.6 points (judge.md). On 30 Sep one task was about 1.7 points and #7-#25 were tied at 0.13 (raw.json). The deadline, 2 Dec (entry 25 Nov), comes before Enveda's 14 Dec. The work is harness and SWE engineering, the assistant's strongest area, and it shares nothing technical with the chemistry, so the conflict is purely one of attention.

findings.claim: RSNA: rented GPUs remove the compute wall but not the time and CV walls. A bronze attempt would cost about 18-20 full days, about 100-150 GPU-h and about $100-400 (estimate). New fit about 3.5 (was 2.5-3). Bronze about 20-30% (was 15-20%), silver about 5%, gold about 0% (estimates). Verdict: still skip.
findings.evidence: There are only 58 expert-labelled train studies; the rest (about 4,349) have report-derived labels (https://huggingface.co/blog/bishnoiyash/rsna-competetion, https://github.com/TranBaDat2607/RSNA-Knee-Abnormality-Detection). A macro AUC over 12 labels on 58 studies is too noisy to choose between models, so the public LB (about 390 studies) would become the judge, which is exactly the Biohub trap. One repo reports gold-58 0.930 vs public 0.939, and the HF blog reports 0.857 on gold after a leak fix vs 0.903 public. The top 50 are at 0.953-0.961 and the best public notebook is 0.946 (raw.json). The GPU need of 60-150+ GPU-h comes from judge.md. At $0.7-2.7/h that is about $100-400; the 5070 Ti can take the 2D/2.5D CNNs, whose models fit in 16 GB (https://www.bestgpusforai.com/gpu-comparison/5070-ti-vs-4090). Entry closes 15 Oct and the final is 22 Oct, which overlaps Enveda days 1-22.

findings.claim: RSNA data transfer: do not move 570 GB. Preprocess inside free Kaggle CPU notebooks into a cache of about 40 GB, keep it as private datasets (no publication needed), and download only that to a rented server.
findings.evidence: The HF blog made a 39 GB cache (288×288, 64 slices, uint8) from about 820k slices in 978 s. Kaggle downloads to cloud GPUs can run at 2 MB/s, or about 12 MB/s with 4 parallel connections (https://www.synpixcloud.com/blog/kaggle-download-slow-cloud-gpu). At those speeds 570 GB takes about 13-80 h plus about $30-100/month of disk; 40 GB takes about 1-5.5 h (estimates). Downloading competition data needs the rules accepted, which is the user's action.

findings.claim: ARC-AGI-2: dev compute makes CV runs off our Kaggle quota cheap, but an own model at NVARC scale does not fit in 33 days. Fit 3.5 → 4. summary:
ENVEDA WITH MORE COMPUTE: the ceiling goes up, but less than the added compute suggests. Budget cap: ~$150-400 of rented GPU. (All probabilities, costs and GPU-hours below are my estimates; bases are given.)

Why more GPU matters. Compute is now roughly 5-20x what the survey assumed. By my estimate, 30 Kaggle GPU-h/week of T4/P100 is only about 3-6 A100-hours. That opens three GPU-heavy parts of the strongest known pipeline that were out of reach on CPU plus Kaggle quota:
1. A fingerprint model trained on the full 2.5M training spectra, either MIST-style or DreaMS fine-tuned.
2. A forward spectrum simulator (ICEBERG, which predicts a spectrum from a structure), fine-tuned on timsTOF. It would simulate spectra for the whole ~1M-structure candidate pool, which turns class-2 molecules into something close to library matches.
3. A time-boxed attempt at class 3 with de novo generation (FRIGID, public Apache-2.0 weights, reported 16-18% top-1 on MassSpecGym).

What is working in the competition now (Discussion, 30 Sep):
- The bottleneck is ranking among same-formula isomers, not recall. About 98% of wrong top-1 picks from the database share the truth's formula.
- Evidence that depends on how atoms connect (in-silico fragmentation) is where gains are coming from.
- Gains under about 0.03 are invisible on the ~130-molecule public LB.
- NIST data or anything trained on it means disqualification. Licences must allow commercial use and redistribution.
- The host confirmed that training on the competition data in a private external cloud is allowed.

Our CV plan needs a fix. The survey's np-examples masks leak: all 250 of those structures also appear in other libraries in train. Masks must therefore remove by InChIKey14 across every library, and should be backed by per-library class-2 panels.

Realistic ceiling (public-LB scale, estimates):
- CPU + Kaggle only: about 0.40-0.42.
- With rented bursts plus the 5070 Ti: about 0.41-0.45, central ~0.425.
- For reference, #1 is 0.464 and the fork plateau is 0.384-0.401.

Medal odds move modestly: bronze from 30-40% to about 40-50%, silver from ~10% to about 15-20%, gold about 3%. The move is modest because the Biohub post-mortem showed attention and domain knowledge, not GPU, were the binding constraint. That is still true here, and the private set (~270 molecules) will shake up rankings.

Plan: an 11-week schedule with CPU-first CV and ranker, two rented-GPU bursts (fingerprint model, then forward simulator), a hard-gated de novo experiment, a code freeze on 8 Dec, and explicit kill criteria at each phase.

Process notes: no Kaggle API calls, nothing clicked, nothing joined or submitted. Chrome was read-only in one new tab, now closed. I made a second ToolSearch call to load read_page, because get_page_text does not return the links to discussion threads.

findings.claim: The live leaderboard confirms the survey: #1 is 0.464, then 0.435 / 0.425 / 0.420; ranks 10-49 are a flat 0.401-0.384 plateau of forks. The public LB is about 33% of test (~130 molecules), and private is the other 67% (~270).
findings.evidence: https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/enveda-CASMI26-molecule-id-mass-spectra/leaderboard (read 30 Sep; the page states 'approximately 33% of the test data').

findings.claim: The remaining errors are mostly isomer-ranking errors, not recall errors. Structure-aware evidence (in-silico fragmentation, i.e. predicting how the molecule breaks) is where the current #5 team finds gains. That team reports: one molecule is worth about 0.0025 MRR; seed noise of the ranker is up to ±0.007; offline gains under ~0.03 were invisible on the public LB; the standard error of the difference between two submissions is about 0.016.
findings.evidence: Udam Liyanage (public #5), 'Lessons from ~30 submissions', https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/enveda-CASMI26-molecule-id-mass-spectra/discussion/743254: when the truth is in the candidate list but not first, the winner has the same formula ~98% of the time; a mass window of 8.5 vs 10 ppm barely matters; PubChem ∪ COCONUT covers what ChEBI/LIPID MAPS/NPAtlas cover. In the same thread, NeckBeard found that tuning on the evaluation panel inflated a fragmentation gain 2.8x (+0.065 → +0.023 held out), and that change did not move the LB (0.341 → 0.336).

findings.claim: The survey's CV design (np-examples with masks A/B/C) leaks. Masks must remove each structure by InChIKey14 across ALL libraries, and CV should be backed by per-library class-2 panels plus a timsTOF natural-product panel.
findings.evidence: https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/enveda-CASMI26-molecule-id-mass-spectra/discussion/741597: all 250 np-examples structures also appear in riken/gnps/mona/massbank/pluskal, so holding out only by library name inflates CV. A participant's LB-probed estimate of the test mix: class 1 ~16%, class 2 ~45%, class 3 ~39%. This is unofficial; the arithmetic in the thread only supports f2 ≈ 18% directly.

findings.claim: The licence rules are tight: NIST, or any model trained on NIST, means disqualification, and solutions must allow commercial use and redistribution. This rules out CSI:FingerID/SIRIUS fingerprints (a proprietary online web service, impossible without internet anyway) and any NIST-trained weights of MassFormer or ICEBERG.
findings.evidence: Host David Healey: https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/enveda-CASMI26-molecule-id-mass-spectra/discussion/744470 ('any solution using or trained on NIST will be disqualified') and the welcome post https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/enveda-CASMI26-molecule-id-mass-spectra/discussion/741359. SIRIUS docs: https://boecker-lab.github.io/docs.sirius.github.io/prerequisites/. ms-pred README: NIST weights require a commercial licence, https://github.com/coleygroup/ms-pred/blob/main/README.md.

findings.claim: Training on rented or cloud GPUs is explicitly allowed by the host. The resulting weights go back into the Kaggle notebook as a dataset or model.
findings.evidence: https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/enveda-CASMI26-molecule-id-mass-spectra/discussion/741876: asked about uploading the training data to a private cloud, training there and using the weights on Kaggle, the host answered 'Yes, you can do that.'

findings.claim: These public, licence-compatible building blocks exist: DreaMS (MIT weights, 1024-d spectrum embeddings, fine-tunable), MassSpecGym (MIT, ~231k spectra), MIST (MIT, NPLIB1 weights), ICEBERG 2.1 MassSpecGym weights, FRIGID (Apache 2.0; MIST encoder + de novo decoder + ICEBERG checkpoints on Zenodo), COCONUT, and PubChem/PubChemLite.
findings.evidence: https://github.com/pluskal-lab/DreaMS (Zenodo 10997887, HF roman-bushuiev/DreaMS); https://huggingface.co/datasets/roman-bushuiev/MassSpecGym; https://github.com/samgoldman97/mist; https://github.com/coleygroup/ms-pred; https://github.com/coleygroup/FRIGID (Zenodo 19685145). Caveat: the licences of NPLIB1/GNPS-derived subsets need a per-source check (estimate).

findings.claim: Method strength (benchmark numbers, not on Enveda data): MIST is the strongest classic spectrum-to-fingerprint retriever on MassSpecGym (R@1 16.3%, R@20 53.2%, vs DeepSets 0.8%/13.5%). Forward simulators are competitive rankers (ICEBERG 25→40% top-1 on NIST20 after its 2.0 changes; FraGNNet ~30%). An audit of MassSpecGym papers found leakage or shortcuts in 17 of 26, so reported numbers are optimistic.
findings.evidence: MassSpecGym: https://arxiv.org/html/2410.23326v1. ICEBERG/FraGNNet: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2404.02360 and https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12154671/. Audit: https://arxiv.org/html/2606.19624v1 (formula-known retrieval: FRIGID Hit@1 45%, ICEBERG 36%/Hit@20 79%, DiffMS 32%).

findings.claim: De novo generation (class 3) is no longer hopeless on benchmarks, but it has not transferred to this LB. FRIGID reports 16-18% top-1 on MassSpecGym and 20-25% on NPLIB1 at ~6.6 s per spectrum, and needs the molecular formula; DiffMS reports 2.3%. Top teams report that generated candidates have not yet paid off on the LB, and that deleting a structure from the database overstates de novo reach about 3x compared with molecules that are genuinely absent.
findings.evidence: FRIGID: https://arxiv.org/html/2604.16648v1 and https://github.com/coleygroup/FRIGID. DiffMS: https://arxiv.org/html/2502.09571v2. MIST+MolForge claims 31% top-1 (https://arxiv.org/html/2508.04180), probably inflated per the audit. LB transfer: discussion/743254.

findings.claim: A forward model (structure → MS/MS) is the most compute-leveraged lever. Simulating the whole ~1M-structure pool is cheap once, and it gives structure-aware evidence for exactly the isomer problem that limits current scores.
findings.evidence: hengck23's hint 'train a smiles to MS/MS predictor too' (https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/enveda-CASMI26-molecule-id-mass-spectra/discussion/744343). ICEBERG 2.0 reports 10.8 ms/spectrum on 2×A5000 (via PMC12154671 search result), so 1M structures × 3 collision energies ≈ 9 h on 2×A5000 ≈ 4-6 A100-h (estimate). Training needs 2 GPUs with ≥24 GB each (ms-pred README), so the 16 GB 5070 Ti is not enough for training; rent for this.

findings.claim: The train/test shift is large: test is 100% timsTOF, while train is 46% timsTOF, 30% Orbitrap and 13% dimer adducts. Instrument-weighted training and fine-tuning on enveda-180 (timsTOF) are where our own models can beat generic public checkpoints.
findings.evidence: https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/enveda-CASMI26-molecule-id-mass-spectra/discussion/744011 (metadata of train vs the visible test: 79% [M+H]+, 16% [M-H]-, precursor m/z 245-460). Caveat from discussion/743254: the visible test.parquet is a placeholder drawn from train.

findings.claim: The relative speed of our hardware changes the arithmetic. RTX 5070 Ti ≈ 0.25-0.35x A100 on transformer training; a Kaggle T4 ≈ 0.1-0.2x A100 (no bf16). So 30 Kaggle GPU-h/week ≈ 3-6 A100-h. The 5070 Ti is Blackwell (sm_120) and needs PyTorch cu128+; DGL, which ms-pred/ICEBERG use, may lack wheels. This is unverified and should be tested on day 1.
findings.evidence: GPT-2 training throughput of about 11.5k vs 50k tokens/s (5070 Ti vs A100), with bf16 peak of about 88 vs 312 TFLOPS, per https://tensorrigs.com/blog/deep-learning-gpu-benchmarks/ and https://gigachadllc.com/geforce-rtx-5070-ti-ai-benchmarks-breakdown/ (third-party). The T4 ratio is my estimate.
